title: Force on a current-carrying wire
log: 2026-10-27T00:53:12Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

draft.title: Force on a current-carrying wire
card: A current is a flow of moving charges. A wire carrying current in a magnetic field therefore feels a force, as each moving charge does.

The size of the force is F = BIL sin θ. B is the field strength in tesla, I is the current in amperes, L is the length of wire in the field in metres, and θ is the angle between the wire and the field.
The force is greatest when the wire is at right angles to the field (θ = 90°). It is zero when the wire runs parallel to the field (θ = 0°).

The force is at right angles to both the wire and the field. For direction, point your right thumb along the conventional current and your fingers along the field. The palm pushes in the direction of the force.
draft.remember: F = BIL sin θ: the force is biggest at 90° to the field and zero when parallel.

a.q: A straight wire carries a current in a uniform magnetic field. For which angle between the wire and the field is the force on the wire zero?
opts: 0°, with the wire parallel to the field
90°, with the wire at right angles to the field
60°, with the wire tilted towards the field
a.why: The force is F = BIL sin θ, and sin 0° = 0. A wire parallel to the field feels no force. At 90° the sine is 1, so that is where the force is greatest, not zero.
a.clue: Check what sin θ equals for each angle.

b.q: A 0.20 m length of wire carries 5.0 A at right angles to a uniform field of 0.30 T. What is the force on the wire?
b.why: F = BIL sin θ = 0.30 × 5.0 × 0.20 × sin 90° = 0.30 N. The value 1.5 N comes from leaving out the length L, which is the tempting mistake.
b.clue: At 90°, sin θ is 1, so multiply B, I and L.

a.best: 0°, with the wire parallel to the field
